newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia PM urges talks on governing rebel bases.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia PM urges talks on governing rebel bases.

text.p: Co-Premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh said on Thursday the way was clear for talks on returning civil administration to this former Khmer Rouge base now that its rebel inhabitants had joined the government.
"The next priority step is to talk about the civil administration," Ranariddh told reporters in the sprawling Malai base on the Thai-Cambodian border.

Hundreds of schoolchildren and villagers greeted the prince on his first visit to Phnom Malai -- home to former Khmer Rouge guerrillas loyal to breakaway leader Ieng Sary -- since the guerrillas split with hardliners in August.

Last week, the Khmer Rouge dissidents pledged their allegiance to Cambodia's coalition government and formally merged their forces with the royal army. Most of the troops wore their new, government-issue uniforms during Ranariddh's visit.
Ranariddh said Thursday the dissident bases of Phnom Malai, Pailin and Samlaut were also now considered once again under the control of the kingdom of Cambodia.
Ranariddh also said the dissident areas would be developed as a separate province and the U.S. government would fund construction of roads into Phnom Malai and Pailin.
Thailand was also willing to help develop the area, Ranariddh said.
Ieng Sary, foreign minister during the genocidal 1975-1979 regime of Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot, escorted the prince to a welcoming ceremony at the run-down Malai secondary school.
Sok Pheap, commander of the Malai-based division 450 said that Ranariddh's visit "seals the biggest national reconciliation, national union and peace ever seen in the history of Cambodia".
The commander also called on "our comrades who, for one reason or another have erred, to return to the fold," an apparent reference to guerrillas still loyal to Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot.
Ranariddh later told reporters the dissidents had met with hardliners on October 26 in an unsuccessful attempt to bring them over to the government side.

Ieng Sary agreed that the establishment of a civil administration in the dissident areas should become the next focal point of reconciliation talks. He told Reuters that the Khmer Rouge's internal problems represented "the start of the end of the war."
The Khmer Rouge, whose disastrous experiment in agrarian reform in the late 1970s killed more than one million Cambodians, have been crippled by mass defections in recent months.
The Maoist guerrilla force is believed to have shrunk to between 800 and 2,000 hardline fighters based at Anlong Veng near the Thai border.
